title: Delhi sees more protests as freed 'cockroach' group's leaders vow to fight on
content: India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the nation's capital sees demonstrations for a second day, with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday. Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated" in his first comments after his release. Media reports said 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday, with hundreds detained on Sunday. The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied. On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said. After his release, Dipke posted on X: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India." He said he was going to his village to attend the funeral of his grandmother, who died around the time of his arrest. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". Ranka and Das later told a news conference that the condition did not mean they could not protest. "Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said. "Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest. Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed. For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded, offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed. In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there were rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. Protesters were vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions. Some were put onto buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants. Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses. The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora , who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained. Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum. "Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding: "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight." The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms. Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue. At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route. Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day. After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday. On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions. The court ordered the government to restore the internet, and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there were a disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention. The row centres on a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide. The commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters. At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed. The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated. The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms. Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he wrote on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" Chief Justice Surya Kant says his cockroach comments were misinterpreted. But Dipke's post went viral and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability. Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister. Opposition leaders allege that CEC Gyanesh Kumar manipulated voter rolls to favour PM Narendra Modi's party. India's street performers are struggling to survive as audiences shrink and public spaces become harder to access. Little-known political parties are receiving millions in donations despite limited electoral activity. As Brics leaders meet in Delhi, divisions within the bloc make a united response to Washington unlikely. It's not clear how many people were inside the building - or if there are still people under the debris. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days
content: One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said. A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack. It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week. The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa. On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4. US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia. Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime". Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled". The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region. Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. A residential home in the city was also struck, killing a child and injuring six people, the media outlet reported. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attacks and the BBC has been unable to verify this report. Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners. Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals . The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport. There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that. The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July. The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions. The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control. Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi Arabian counterpart on Sunday that his country was ready to provide assistance to "facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen", referring to the Houthi administration. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict. The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies. The BBC reports from a school in Taiz, Yemen, where children are determined to keep learning despite the vicious civil war. Saudi-backed forces gave conflicting reports of whether they had also seized the port city of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
content: At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says. Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday. Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented. Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border. Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region. "The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes." It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise. The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured. Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote. The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers. Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining. At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens. Gold lies at the core of the border tensions. Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders. Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels. Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment. Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups. This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market. After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill. Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says. Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
content: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said. The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says. The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered. "This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives." Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them. Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change. Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti. IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families". The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added. More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics. In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's. The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month. Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen. After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles. The Saudi capital has been hit by multiple attacks from the Iran-backed Yemeni group over the weekend. All asylum applications would be rejected and existing ones voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. Neither Egypt nor Sudan has commented on the alleged strikes on an artisanal mining camp on Saturday. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
content: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found. During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force. BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles. Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones. In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones. The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives. Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots. Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures. A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account. The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute. "The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said. Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment." Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said. Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home. The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked. After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful. In total, three people were killed. One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head. The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion. Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head. Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered. Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons. The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection. The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium. Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment. Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join. Within hours, he was dead. His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans. As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government. "I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said. "It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him." Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent. Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica , on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill. The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya. The patient had been living in DR Congo, where more than 4,000 people have died from the disease this year. Kennington residents fundraise for the much-needed resource which will open on 10 October. A voter mobilisation campaign has registered huge numbers of young people but it is not clear who they are backing. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
content: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children. "These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools. A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw. It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker. "We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added. The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right. "Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online". On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian. A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone". Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge. Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said. A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious". Polish police had already deployed to schools after a female caretaker was killed and several others injured in two earlier attacks in two days. Police say they foiled another school attack on Thursday, and a day after a stabbing at another Polish school. Robert Lewandowski, 38, scores a hat-trick in the Nations League and Edin Dzeko plays his final game for Bosnia-Herzegovina. A male suspect from Ukraine was arrested after the stabbings in the town of Jarosław, police say. The satellite station is used in part to provide internet coverage to neighbouring Ukraine, the government says. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Takeaways from the South Carolina Senate debate
content: South Carolina has emerged as perhaps the most surprising Senate race to be competitive late in the 2026 midterm elections. And on Sunday night, appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian nominee Kasie Whitener took part in the only debate currently scheduled in the race. The debate was often contentious, with both Graham and Andrews taking aim at each other. Andrews focused on the idea that Graham — the late former Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom President Donald Trump plucked from obscurity to succeed him — is the choice of political insiders and not running a serious campaign. She at one point alluded to an embarrassing moment at a primary runoff debate in which Graham said, “National security is not my thing.” “If your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.” Graham also hit Andrews early and often, seeking to tie her to the political left. And she repeatedly took offense to the attacks that Andrews lodged, accusing Andrews of going after her family. Below are some takeaways from the debate. Job No. 1 for Graham was avoiding a moment like the one on national security. And she cleared that bar. At that GOP debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, she was asked a relatively basic — at least for a senator — question about US foreign policy interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Seemingly not knowing where to go with it, she just admitted that she didn’t know much about the issue. At the same debate, she also mistakenly cited 50 million people living in South Carolina, when the actual number is less than 6 million. That doesn’t mean Sunday was smooth sailing. Graham paused awkwardly at times. She struggled to make some of her attack lines, such as on transgender rights, land. Some of her claims — like that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel launched the war earlier this year — don’t actually appear true. But for a Republican running in a pretty red state, she came across as more capable than before. That being said, Graham seemed to confirm that her campaign is quite concerned about Andrews, judging by how much time she spent attacking the Democrat. It started almost instantly, with Graham calling Andrews “most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina” in her first answer. She accused Andrews of supporting government-run healthcare, which Andrews denied. She pointed to Andrews’ past work on gun control issues. She attacked Andrews for opposing President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and for having the support of Jane Fonda’s political action committee. And after Andrews mentioned her primary runoff debate moment, Graham accused her of lying about her liberal positions. “Let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing, apparently, is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” she said. “But you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove different. Shame on you.” The attacks confirmed the competitiveness of the race. The national GOP recently turned heads by spending $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign. But Andrews had a pretty memorable answer for much of it. “She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani; that’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said, referring to a trio of democratic socialist lawmakers. “But the truth is: My name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.” Graham opted not to use her married name — Darline Graham Nordone — when she was appointed as a senator. “My legal name is Graham and has always been Graham,” she said. “And you know why it’s Graham? Because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.” At another point in the debate, Andrews said that “both parties have failed on immigration” and that “Democrats have failed on the border.” Andrews added: “And the truth is, I support the Second Amendment. I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law, and yes, I want to lower taxes on the middle class.” Few attacks have been as central to the race as the GOP’s efforts to focus on transgender issues. Just in the last week, Trump posted on social media using an anti-transgender slur for Andrews, and Andrews launched a direct-to-camera ad defending herself on the issue. But if you blinked, you might have missed it Sunday night. Graham brought it up twice, but only briefly. And she did so both times at the end of an answer, right before the debate quickly moved on. That included at the very end of the debate. “But let’s talk about a couple of other concerns I have — that she’s deceiving the people of South Carolina with these transgender issues,” Graham said in the final words of the night. The debate moderator quickly signaled the debate had to end there, and it was over. That was a win for Andrews, in that she didn’t really have to answer for the issue — or explain her 2022 comments on social media calling a state law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools “shameful.” Andrews repeatedly pointed to Graham declining to vote with Democrats and a few Republicans to bringing the Iran war to an end, noting Graham has had three chances to do so. Graham responded by claiming that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon — which is not backed up by known US intelligence. But unlike some GOP Senate candidates who have said the war needs to end, she went a little further in defending the need to give Trump more time. She argued Iran is being strangled financially. “Why in the world would we stop now when they are still dangerous and we are close to ending the war?” Graham said. “Again, I think the president wants to end the war. I know he does. We all want the war to end. But I support a strong military. I believe in peace through strength.” Few things loomed as large over the debate as Trump; his unpopularity is a major reason South Carolina and other deep-red states are as competitive this fall. But he wasn’t a major focus. There was the occasional mention of something Trump has done, but he wasn’t really a focal point for anybody. In fact, the word “Trump” was only uttered a handful of times. Graham mentioned the president just a few times, praising him for creating an AI task force and waiving restrictions on red-dye diesel . Even when Andrews was arguing Graham was the pick of insiders, she didn’t actually cite the one insider above all who elevated Graham: Trump. And when talking about the war, she generally didn’t attach it to the president. That perhaps shouldn’t be too surprising from the Democrat. While Trump is broadly unpopular nationwide, this is still a state he won by 18 points in 2024.

title: Judge orders Trump to halt taxpayer-funded ads with hours left in administration’s push
content: A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda. Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court. The Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET. Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads. The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection , CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case. The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month . On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC. But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing. The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads. In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.” The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted. The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.” CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group. Mehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN. And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.” A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund. The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.) Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded. “Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths. “We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.” This story and headline have been updated with additional developments.

title: Raphael Warnock has a message for Democrats — and a plan to be heard in 2028
content: As a boy, Raphael Warnock started offering a prayer: that God would guide his feet, order his steps and direct his path. Maybe, he says, it grew out of the verses in Proverbs that say pretty much the same. Now that path had taken him to New Hampshire, the state politicians go to when they want people to start thinking of them running for president. “I don’t have any kind of hocus-pocus, spooky spirituality. It’s a faith that’s grounded in real life. It requires analysis, deep thought,” the Georgia Democratic senator told CNN shortly after arriving. “It respects data and science and hard work, but beneath all of that is an abiding sense that I’m a part of something that’s bigger than me.” “My prayer is that I can be used to do the most good with the gifts that I have,” Warnock said. “And I hope that at the end of the day, at the end of my life, I want to leave it all on the field.” Warnock’s friend and fellow Georgia senator, Jon Ossoff, immediately shuts down all speculation about whether he’ll run for president. Warnock very much does not, other than to say that he wants to make sure Democrats get through this year’s midterms first. He is making campaign stops to boost Democratic allies while test-driving a 2028 message that critiques both parties on faith and character. “The Democratic Party’s like most old institutions. It’s slow to change. I feel that institutional inertia and I refuse to be bound by it, so I’m going to keep pushing this because what we’re faced with is so much bigger than party,” Warnock said. “Old-school politicians who’ve been at this for a while, they have a certain way that they’re accustomed to doing this. And that way doesn’t lead to a Raphael Warnock in the Senate.” There are two dozen or more Democrats planning a presidential run or being pushed to consider one. But there’s only one member of the party who is the 11th of 12 children of two Pentecostal ministers in Savannah, a Black senator who unseated a Republican in a red state, who has staff who can rattle off passages from Isaiah from spending time around him, and who has colleagues asking him for spiritual advice. “They ask me to pray, and some need more prayer than others,” he jokes. As he spoke to CNN, he stood across the street from the City Hall steps where John F. Kennedy kicked off his presidential campaign on a cold day in 1960. It was Warnock’s first time in New Hampshire. His day included a coffeehouse stop in Portsmouth, a lunch of barbecue chicken tenders at a firehouse, and an evening opening of a campaign office with people pouring into the hallway and out the backdoor of a space wedged between a consignment furniture store and a Brazilian jiu-jitsu parlor. Crowds that didn’t look like his congregation back in Atlanta or sound like Georgia voters pressed in to hear. “He was definitely connecting,” New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley told CNN afterward, noting that in his decades of watching presidential hopefuls make their pilgrimages to the state, “that’s not always a given in New Hampshire.” “I think that there’s great interest in him,” Buckley added, “and the interesting thing, of course, is that there’s also great interest in Ossoff.” Driving along the changing leaves and lakes, snacking on the lobster roll that aides picked up for him, Warnock was officially on the ground to campaign for House candidate Stefany Shaheen and Senate candidate Chris Pappas. He ripped into tariffs as the biggest tax any person had ever put on the “Live Free or Die” state and spoke at length on how “Donald Trump has unleashed a kind of evil and wickedness into the ether.” But he also told a story of Lyndon B. Johnson passing the Civil Rights Act and then telling Martin Luther King Jr. he didn’t have the power to pass a voting rights bill: “If the president doesn’t have the power,” Warnock says King said, “we’re going to have to go get him some.” Warnock’s sense of fitting into something bigger, he said several times in New Hampshire, was reaffirmed by how he arrived in Washington: He and Ossoff winning runoffs the day before the January 6 riots at the Capitol, giving Democrats a slim Senate majority that they eventually used to pass an expanded child tax credit and to confirm Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court. As a politician and a pastor, Warnock revs up crowds with his call to action, “Keep marching!” Most Sundays, he is back delivering his sermon at Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church in King’s old pulpit. But he’s had his own difficult time. He has a biting joke about investigating Jesus for identity theft on the Senate floor (“I don’t know who these people are talking about”). He also senses such a deep ache in his congregation that last month he delivered a series of sermons on trauma, of people hit so hard over the last 10 years that “wherever I go, whether I’m in Georgia or New Hampshire, there’s always just beneath the surface, even in happier moments, this heaviness.” Over breakfast in Portsmouth, Warnock said he’s had what he calls his own labors of despair living through these years of American politics. “Any thinking person of faith living through a moment like this has some questions for God: ‘Why are we here? I can’t believe we’re doing this again,’” Warnock said. “And I’m comfortable there because as I read the scripture that actually puts me in good company with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, a Jewish kid from Nazareth named Jesus.” Warnock sees himself on a mission to redeem the soul of America — whether that’s on the Senate floor, blasting what he sees as Republicans using performative moments of prayer to cover for what he sees as immoral policy since “the prophets had harsh words for that kind of religion”; pushing Democratic leaders to reorient which candidates they invest in; or traveling over the final weeks of this election cycle to at least three of his party’s early presidential primary states. “God is not a Democrat. And contrary to what people seem to think, God is not a Republican,” Warnock said. “God is on the side of that single mother who’s trying to figure out how she can afford daycare so she can go to work or get a job so she can afford a daycare in a country where we just spend enough money in the war in Iran to provide pre-K for every 4-year-old in America. I think God’s on the side of seniors who are having to decide whether they’re going to buy groceries or buy medicine.” Told that Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito writes in his upcoming book that the decision to legalize gay marriage was “perhaps the decisive point in our nation’s turn against religious liberty,” Warnock stopped and stared in apparent disbelief. “What about slavery?” he said. “You know what I think is an insult to God? Any form of human domination over others.” In Keene, Warnock smiled as he said he was making his high school English teacher proud by referencing Robert Frost’s two diverging roads to describe the choice he sees for the country in 2028. He’ll have to make his own choice, too. Between a primary, general elections and runoffs, Warnock ran five tough, expensive, down-to-the-wire elections over two years in 2020 and 2022—first for the remainder of a term and then for a full one — which means his seat is up in 2028. “That’s a moment, and I do think that ’28 will be a moment that’s even bigger than the election cycle itself,” Warnock told CNN. “I think it will be about the character of the nation, like what kind of country do we want to be.” Most of the Democrats looking at running for president have standard lines about how they’re only focused on 2026. Warnock has his fallbacks too, in part around trying to reorient which candidates his party takes seriously, and where. For months, he’s been pushing for more attention to the Mississippi Senate race and Democratic nominee Scott Colom, who is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. He cites how there are more Black voters in Mississippi than in Georgia and said he tried to get donors to look at the race. He’s clearly frustrated that some of those making decisions write him off as a well-meaning leader with Sen. Chuck Schumer’s cellphone number but still a relative political newbie. Warnock will go to Mississippi on Wednesday to campaign for Colom, but also to hold roundtable discussions with Black men. Warnock walks into rooms with a politician’s ease and a pastor’s cadence. In Portsmouth, he told a boy with Down syndrome named Michael that they were both named after angels. In Nashua, he told an older White woman wearing a Jesse Jackson ’88 button, which she got on the civil rights leader’s tour of the state, that she was coming to him with one of his idols. In Keene, he talked about the famous story of the rabbi who said that Jewish teaching boils down to treating others the way you’d want to be treated, and how that is what so many faiths have in common. Pappas, who doesn’t tend to dominate rooms the same way, told CNN that what sets Warnock apart from the other potential presidential candidates who have come through New Hampshire is that the senator “provides a moral perspective that’s really important for our politics right now.” “He achieved unbelievable victory in his two Senate races that he ran within just a few years of each other,” Pappas said. “People in New Hampshire know that example of being a coalition builder, of being a voice that matters right now.” Some aides and advisers don’t want Warnock to give up his seat to chase this dream, hoping the analysis will lead to prayers that lead to him filing for reelection. Warnock said he hasn’t started having those real conversations with them, or with his family, including his two young children with his ex-wife. “Look, I know that in a matter of months,” he said, “I’ll be in a race.”

title: Trump really wants to make ‘super intelligence’ happen. Is it going to happen?
content: Unable to convince Americans to embrace the AI data centers they hate , President Donald Trump is instead exercising the one power he believes is absolute in the presidency: a rebrand. But unlike Lake America , the Gulf of America, military bases or a mountain, this change is about altering public opinion rather than scoring political points. Trump first told fellow world leaders at the United Nations last month that “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake.” After Trump signed an executive order in late September, the US government has been changing official documents and websites. Cabinet secretaries and other aides immediately used the new term. Elon Musk said on X that he would change the name of his company from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, although that particular change has not yet occurred. Trump has refused to answer questions that use the old term. He told supporters at a campaign rally in Nebraska that he would henceforth repurpose “artificial” — an “ugly” word, he said — for the news media. On Thursday, the president said on social media that anyone who uses the term artificial intelligence instead of super intelligence will be viewed by his White House as “THE ENEMY!” All of this might feel very much like Trump’s “weave” — the mental meanderings of Trump’s public statements — but it has also been fascinating to watch the infrastructure of the federal government respond to what many Americans might write off as a semantic distinction. There are things that are out of Trump’s power — passing spending bills, renaming the Kennedy Center, ending his war against Iran — but he has shown that presidents have power to change names. It’s also evidence he knows the unpopularity of data centers and concerns about AI in general at a time when he is a major booster of AI. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long pushed to view AI as superintelligence. In August, he published a 6,000-word treatise about how Meta would approach AI. In rose assessments of the future, he referred to the promise of superintelligence. When he referred to AI, it was usually in reference to what he argued were unfounded worries. Zuckerberg said Meta will be committed to an open source model that provides for superintelligent agents working on behalf of every individuals. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico’s “Decoded” podcast there are no plans to change the name of his company to OpenSI. But he did say that people in the industry have been using the term superintelligence for a while. It might be a better term, ultimately, than artificial intelligence, but “still sort of understates the magnitude of what I think is happening,” Altman said. Altman predicted people would still use the term AI and questioned whether Trump’s rebrand would accomplish its goal of changing people’s opinions of AI. “Does superintelligence sound obviously less scary to people than artificial intelligence?” Altman wondered. Time will tell. What is definitely true is that the concept of superintelligence, while it sounds better in Trump’s view, is arguably distinct from AI and should be no less intimidating to Americans. The term artificial intelligence has its roots in the 1950s, when a group of Dartmouth professors held a summertime conference “on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” Superintelligence, at least academically, seems more like the next step of artificial intelligence, or artificial generative intelligence. That happens when the machines learn. The Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom has written extensively about superintelligence, including in the 2014 book “Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies.” Here’s how Bostrum first defined superintelligence in a 1997 essay: Asked how he views Trump’s rebrand, Bostrum said that from a technical perspective AI has traditionally “been this wide umbrella term that refers to every form of intelligent information processing in machines.” We’re talking everything from the Google searches and email spam filters, the current crop of AIs and “hypothetical future more powerful ones.” “If the idea is to use the new word superintelligence to cover all of that, it’s a little bit of a stretch, maybe, to call my spam filter a superintelligence,” Bostrum told CNN. In the theoretical evolution of AI, what comes next, he said is AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which refers to a system that has the same kind of learning and reasoning as humans, something Atman says might already have occurred. “Superintelligence was reserved for this sort of hypothetical future form of artificial intelligence that not only matched but radically exceeded humans across all cognitive domain,” according to Bostrum. That is exactly the thing that frightens the AI “doomers.” But it is incomprehensible to Trump that the machines could outwit him. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote in September, arguing against any sort of AI regulation. Bostrum has written both about potential pitfalls of superintelligence as well as the enormous potential to improve and extend human life. But by changing the name, Trump seems to just want to control the narrative. Bostrum doesn’t necessarily think it’s a bad idea. “It’s not up to me to decide how English language should be used,” he said. “I mean, it’s good for my book sales, I guess.” He does see the rhetorical argument for a new term: It’s harder to argue against super intelligence than artificial intelligence. “If you define superintelligence as we already have superintelligence and it hasn’t caused any catastrophe yet, then what’s the big deal? And you then would need to introduce some new term to refer to this like hypothetical future capability that’s even more powerful.” Trump knows a thing or two about saying things so much that they take hold in the public. He rarely speaks in public without repeating the same talking points about “fake” news, the “radical left” Democrats, or about how wonderful his own leadership has been, regardless of what the facts are. At the UN, Trump compared his rebrand to the evolution of “global warming,” which he said was “reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.” That’s not exactly what happened, as anyone paying attention to the warming climate in recent years can pretty easily confirm.

title: Andy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City
content: Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, had urged the prime minister to publish everything related to his work with the club as Greater Manchester mayor and the Liberal Democrats wrote to him asking him to release minutes of meetings and declare all hospitality gifts received from owners of Manchester City. City has been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club has maintained its innocence and appealed against the verdict. Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”. Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment was serious and that where wrongdoing was established, those responsible should face the consequences. Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday. He said “the football issues are different from the investment issues”. “But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do. “I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester. “None of it is recent … in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting … and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there. “But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.” The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd, which owned the club. The shadow sports minister, Louie French, called for Burnham to also “come clean” about any meetings since becoming prime minister and urged Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, to respond to questions. “The prime minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into No 10, the prime minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full.”
